cues.text: Welcome to Purification and Analysis.
This recorded Chemistry class uses an AI generated Marin voice.
Purification separates a desired substance from impurities by exploiting
differences in properties.
It does not normally change the desired compound into a new chemical.
A mixture of an insoluble solid and a solution may be filtered, but filtering
a
dissolved impurity does not remove it merely because its particles are
invisible.
Qualitative analysis asks which elements or groups are present; quantitative
analysis measures how much.
Characterisation may combine composition with physical or chemical
behaviour.
A sharp melting range can support purity for a suitable solid, but one
measurement alone does not prove identity or perfect purity under every
circumstance.
Consider sand mixed with a dissolved salt solution.
Filtering can retain the sand while the salt remains in the filtrate.
Recovering that dissolved salt requires another principle, such as removing
solvent or crystallizing under suitable conditions.
The proposed method should identify which component is retained, which moves
to
another phase and whether the desired compound's chemical identity is
preserved.
A suitable recrystallization solvent dissolves much of the desired solid when
hot and less when cold, allowing crystals to form on cooling.
Impurities may remain in solution or be removed as insoluble material at a
suitable stage.
The choice must avoid unwanted chemical reaction with the compound.
Cooling does not force every last molecule into crystals; some desired product
remains dissolved, so yield and purity are different goals.
If the solvent dissolves the product equally well hot and cold, simple cooling
is less useful.
Sublimation instead exploits a solid's ability to enter the vapour phase and
redeposit, separating it from suitably nonvolatile impurities.
Suppose a stated solvent quantity dissolves ten grams of a compound when hot
but only two grams at the final cold temperature.
Starting from a hot saturated solution, at most eight grams could crystallize
in that simplified model before additional losses.
A larger recovered mass is not automatically purer material.
Solubility data, solvent quantity and final temperature are necessary before
calculating a theoretical recovery.
Distillation vaporizes part of a liquid mixture and condenses the vapour.
A more volatile component is often enriched in that vapour.
Simple distillation suits some widely separated boiling behaviour or removal
of
a volatile liquid from nonvolatile material; closer boiling liquids may
require
fractional distillation with repeated vapour liquid contact.
Reduced pressure distillation lowers the boiling temperature and can help
avoid
thermal decomposition.
Steam distillation applies to suitable water immiscible, steam volatile
compounds because their vapour pressures contribute to the total.
No method guarantees separation of every mixture: azeotropes and chemical
instability can limit ordinary distillation.
Boiling occurs when the relevant vapour pressure reaches the external
pressure.
Lowering external pressure can therefore reduce the required temperature.
A fractionating column provides repeated separation opportunities rather than
acting as a chemical reagent.
Choose the method from volatility, thermal stability and mixture behaviour,
and
recognize when an azeotrope prevents the assumed unlimited enrichment by
ordinary fractional distillation.
Differential extraction distributes a solute between suitable immiscible
solvents.
The amount in each phase depends on its affinity and the phase volumes;
repeated smaller extractions can be more effective than one extraction of the
same total solvent volume under an appropriate partition model.
Do not assume every organic substance must prefer the organic phase.
Chromatography separates components because they interact differently with
stationary and mobile phases.
In elementary paper or thin layer work, R f is the distance travelled by the
spot divided by the distance travelled by the solvent front from the same
starting line.
It depends on the system and conditions, so matching one R f alone does not
prove identity.
If a chromatographic spot travels three centimetres and the solvent front five
centimetres from the same origin, the ratio is zero point six.
Both distances use the same length units.
Those units cancel, so the ratio is dimensionless.
A new solvent or stationary phase can change the value for the same compound.
In extraction, always state which phase is being analysed and include the
phase
volumes when translating a concentration ratio into recovered amounts.
In organic compounds an element can be covalently bound and not respond
directly as a free ion.
Classical sodium fusion analysis converts suitable nitrogen, sulfur or halogen
content into ionic products that can be tested.
The chemistry involves reactive metal and hazardous products and belongs only
in a supervised laboratory, not an improvised home experiment.
Nitrogen can be detected through cyanide derived iron complex chemistry,
sulfur
through sulfide chemistry and halogens through suitable silver halide
precipitation after removing interferences.
Simultaneous nitrogen and sulfur can form thiocyanate, altering the expected
observations.
Phosphorus detection can involve oxidation to phosphate followed by a suitable
phosphate test.
A negative poorly performed test is not proof an element is absent.
Classical element tests first transform covalently bound elements into species
with recognizable reactions.
This explains why directly adding an ionic test reagent to an untreated
organic
compound may fail.
A positive observation needs the expected chemistry and interference controls;
a negative observation also depends on successful conversion and detection.
Treat the test result as evidence within a stated analytical scheme rather
than
an infallible label.
Complete combustion analysis can relate collected products to carbon and
hydrogen in a sample.
Carbon is measured through carbon dioxide, while hydrogen is measured through
water.
With carbon atomic mass twelve and oxygen sixteen, carbon accounts for twelve
forty fourths of the carbon dioxide mass.
With hydrogen one, hydrogen accounts for two eighteenths of water mass.
Convert product masses to element masses before dividing by sample mass to
obtain percentages.
Only assign the remaining mass to oxygen when the problem establishes that no
other unmeasured element or impurity contributes.
A zero point three zero zero gram sample gives zero point four four zero gram
carbon dioxide and zero point one eight zero gram water.
These correspond to zero point one two zero gram carbon and zero point zero
two
zero gram hydrogen.
Under the stated carbon hydrogen oxygen assumption, oxygen mass is zero point
one six zero gram.
The masses add back to the sample mass.
The carbon percentage is forty and the hydrogen percentage about six point six
seven.
Product mass can exceed sample mass because oxygen from combustion also enters
those products.
Dumas nitrogen estimation measures nitrogen gas after suitable conversion and
removal of interfering gases.
The measured gas volume needs stated temperature, pressure and appropriate
corrections.
Kjeldahl analysis estimates nitrogen through conversion to ammonium and
subsequent ammonia measurement, but does not work without modification for
every nitrogen containing functional group.
Classical Carius type halogen estimation converts suitable halogen content to
a
weighed silver halide; the halogen fraction follows its molar mass share in
that precipitate.
Sulfur can similarly be estimated through sulfate precipitation, and
phosphorus
through an appropriate phosphate derived measurement.
These are stoichiometric principles, not instructions for hazardous digestion
or pressure vessel operation.
For nitrogen gas collected over water, the pressure of water vapour must be
considered before applying the gas law to dry nitrogen.
For a weighed silver halide, the halogen amount follows a molar mass fraction
rather than equality with the whole precipitate mass.
Each method has its own conversion chemistry, so a calculation valid for
carbon
dioxide cannot simply be reused for every analytical product.
Convert each element mass or percentage to moles using its atomic mass, then
divide all amounts by the smallest.
Find a simple integer ratio without rounding a genuine fraction away: a ratio
near one to one and a half may need multiplication by two.
The empirical formula describes the simplest atom ratio.
To find a molecular formula, divide the independently known molar mass by the
empirical formula mass.
A suitable result is an integer multiplier, within the precision of the data.
Multiplying every empirical subscript gives the molecular formula; it still
does not uniquely identify structure.
Report assumptions and rounding rather than forcing inconsistent data into a
familiar compound.
An empirical unit with one carbon, two hydrogens and one oxygen has
approximate
formula mass thirty using the stated rounded atomic masses.
If independent molar mass is ninety, the multiplier is three, giving three
carbons, six hydrogens and three oxygens.
Multiplying only one subscript would change the elemental ratio and fail the
original analysis.
Molecular formula still leaves possible structural isomers.
Dumas style nitrogen analysis requires the amount of dry nitrogen gas, not an
uncorrected wet gas volume at an assumed standard condition.
Suppose supplied results for a zero point two five zero gram suitable sample
give twenty point zero millilitres nitrogen collected over water at three
hundred kelvin.
Total pressure is one hundred kilopascals and the supplied water vapour
pressure is three point zero zero kilopascals.
The nitrogen partial pressure is therefore ninety seven point zero
kilopascals.
Convert the volume to zero point zero two zero zero litre and use R eight
point
three one four litre kilopascal per mole kelvin.
The ideal gas calculation gives about zero point zero zero zero seven seven
seven eight mole nitrogen molecules.
Each molecule contains two nitrogen atoms, so the nitrogen mass uses molar
mass
twenty eight grams per mole of gas, giving about zero point zero two one eight
gram.
Relative to the sample, nitrogen is about eight point seven one percent.
Assume quantitative conversion and gas collection with no other gases present
after the stated analytical treatment.
If the gas is already dry, do not subtract water pressure again.
Temperature, pressure units and the two nitrogen atoms per molecule must all
be
handled explicitly.
A Kjeldahl style numerical problem counts ammonia formed from nitrogen that
the
stated method converts quantitatively.
Use supplied results for a zero point five zero zero gram suitable sample.
Its ammonia is captured by twenty five point zero millilitres of zero point
one
zero zero molar hydrochloric acid.
The remaining acid requires ten point zero millilitres of zero point one zero
zero molar sodium hydroxide.
Initial acid amount is two point five zero millimoles and the residual amount
one point zero zero millimole.
The difference, one point five zero millimoles, equals captured ammonia and
therefore nitrogen atom amount in this model.
Multiplying by fourteen gives zero point zero two one zero gram nitrogen, or
four point two zero percent of the original sample.
Using all the initial acid would overestimate nitrogen.
The standard textbook method is not generally applicable to nitrogen in nitro
or azo groups or pyridine type rings without appropriate modification;
quantitative conversion cannot be assumed for every nitrogen compound.
These are interpretation and stoichiometry steps for supplied analytical data,
not a procedure for carrying out hazardous digestion or handling laboratory
reagents.
Gravimetric halogen analysis measures a compound containing the halogen, not a
pure mass of the halogen itself.
Suppose a supplied halogen analysis result says zero point two zero zero gram
of a suitable chlorine containing organic sample yields zero point one four
three five gram silver chloride.
Assume the collected solid is pure dry silver chloride and the conversion and
recovery are quantitative.
With supplied molar masses one hundred forty three point five for silver
chloride and thirty five point five for chlorine, the precipitate amount is
zero point zero zero one zero zero mole.
Each formula unit contains one chlorine, so chlorine mass is zero point zero
three five five gram.
The sample chlorine percentage is seventeen point seven five.
Do not treat the entire silver chloride mass as chlorine or divide by chlorine
gas molar mass seventy one when counting individual chlorine atoms in the
salt.
Different halogens require the corresponding silver halide molar mass, and
mixed precipitates need additional information.
Contamination, light induced changes or incomplete recovery can invalidate the
simple mass conversion.
This chapter uses reported results and chemical accounting; it does not
provide
a sealed tube experimental recipe.
Repeated solvent portions can remove more solute than one extraction using the
same total solvent volume.
Consider a neutral solute with constant partition ratio K equal to organic
concentration divided by aqueous concentration, taking value four.
Assume two immiscible phases with unchanged volumes, complete equilibration,
no
reaction or ionization and negligible mutual solubility.
Begin with one hundred millilitres aqueous phase.
A single fresh twenty five millilitre organic portion leaves aqueous fraction
one hundred divided by one hundred plus four times twenty five, or one half.
Now use two fresh twelve point five millilitre portions in sequence,
separating
each organic portion before the next contact.
Each leaves fraction one hundred divided by one hundred plus fifty, or two
thirds, of the solute then present in water.
After both, the remaining fraction is four ninths, so about fifty five point
six percent has been extracted rather than fifty percent.
The second contact acts on the remainder, not the original amount.
This calculation assumes a fixed partition ratio for the specified chemical
form; changing p H or allowing association can require a more complete
distribution model.
Chromatography compares movement under specified stationary phase, mobile
phase
and experimental conditions.
Suppose the solvent front travels five point zero zero centimetres while two
sample spots travel two point zero zero and three point five zero centimetres
from the same origin.
Their retention factors are zero point four zero and zero point seven zero.
Both ratios are dimensionless and use the solvent front distance rather than
the plate height or the distance between spots.
A reference substance with retention factor zero point four zero under the
same
conditions supports a possible assignment of the first spot, but matching one
value does not uniquely prove chemical identity.
Different compounds can migrate together, and an apparently single spot does
not guarantee absolute purity.
Changing solvent composition or using another suitable analytical method can
supply independent evidence.
When calculating recovery, compare recovered analyte mass with the amount
originally present; the mass of an isolated fraction can include solvent or
impurities.
Keep separation, recovery and identification as distinct claims.
Record the run conditions and the observed number of resolved components
rather
than treating a familiar retention factor as an invariant molecular constant.
Gravimetric elemental analysis converts an element into a product of known
composition and measures that product mass.
In a supplied quantitative sulfur model, all sample sulfur is recovered in
pure
dry barium sulfate.
Use molar masses barium sulfate two hundred thirty three and sulfur thirty two
grams per mole.
A zero point two zero zero gram sample gives zero point two three three gram
barium sulfate.
Product amount is zero point zero zero one zero zero mole, and each formula
unit contains one sulfur atom, so the sulfur amount is the same.
Sulfur mass is zero point zero three two zero gram, giving sixteen percent of
the original sample mass.
Do not assign the entire precipitate mass to sulfur; most of it is barium and
oxygen.
The calculation assumes complete conversion, quantitative collection and the
specified dry product.
Retained moisture or unrelated coprecipitated material would bias an actual
mass, while incomplete collection could lower recovery.
These supplied data assumptions connect an observation to a composition
calculation.
They are not an experimental oxidation or precipitation procedure.
A gravimetric product can contain more than one atom of the element being
estimated.
In a supplied phosphorus analysis model, all sample phosphorus is recovered as
pure dry magnesium pyrophosphate.
Its formula contains two magnesium, two phosphorus and seven oxygen atoms.
Use supplied molar mass two hundred twenty two grams per mole and phosphorus
atomic mass thirty one.
Suppose a zero point three one zero gram sample gives zero point two two two
gram of the specified product.
That is zero point zero zero one zero zero mole product, containing zero point
zero zero two zero zero mole phosphorus atoms.
Phosphorus mass is zero point zero six two zero gram and its sample mass
percentage is twenty.
Using one phosphorus atom per product unit would halve the answer incorrectly.
Likewise, a different weighed form would require its own formula factor rather
than reuse this conversion unchanged.
Quantitative recovery and a defined dry product are assumptions, and this
numerical model does not supply hazardous sample conversion steps.
Start from the product formula and the counted atom before writing a shortcut
percentage expression.
An elemental percentage obtained by difference is conditional on what the
remainder can contain.
Suppose a dry sample contains only carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen, sulfur and
oxygen.
Supplied measured mass percentages are sixty, eight, twelve and four for the
first four elements respectively.
They sum to eighty four, leaving sixteen percent oxygen under the stated
complete composition model.
A half gram sample would then contain zero point zero eight zero gram oxygen.
Unmeasured halogens, inorganic residue or retained water would make the same
subtraction an unreliable oxygen determination unless separately accounted
for.
All percentages must also refer to the same sample basis; mixing dry basis
carbon with a wet basis sample mass breaks the balance.
Difference calculations combine measurement uncertainty.
If the four supplied small worst case bounds are zero point three, zero point
one, zero point two and zero point one percentage points, their conservative
sum is zero point seven percentage points for the inferred oxygen fraction.
This is not automatically a statistical standard deviation.
State the composition model, sample basis and uncertainty interpretation along
with the remainder.
Steam distillation of a suitable immiscible pair uses the vapour pressures
contributed by both liquid phases at the same temperature.
In an idealized supplied example, the organic component contributes ten
kilopascals and water ninety.
Their sum is one hundred kilopascals, so the mixture can boil against that
external pressure while both liquid phases remain present.
The vapour organic mole fraction is one tenth.
The mole ratio of organic vapour to water vapour is one to nine.
A mass ratio also needs molar masses.
With organic molar mass one hundred eighty and water eighteen grams per mole,
organic mass divided by water mass is ten times one hundred eighty divided by
ninety times eighteen, or ten ninths.
Thus a representative condensed fraction containing ten grams water would
contain about eleven point one grams organic component under this model.
Applying liquid mole fractions as though the liquids formed one ideal miscible
solution would describe a different model.
Phase exhaustion, appreciable mutual solubility, entrainment or chemical
instability can invalidate the simple ratio.
Keep phase presence, vapour composition and condensed mass accounting
explicit.
A silver containing precipitate is not automatically proof that an organic
sample contained a halogen.
In the classical converted extract model, chloride gives silver chloride, but
sulfide and cyanide can also consume silver ions and form precipitates.
The sulfide equation needs two silver ions per sulfide because the charges are
plus one and minus two.
Cyanide forms silver cyanide in a one to one ion ratio.
The analytical scheme must therefore address those interferences before
interpreting a silver halide result.
Acid choice also matters.
Hydrochloric acid introduces chloride ions itself, so it can create a false
chloride signal in a silver test.
A specified nitric acid treatment avoids introducing that particular halide
and
belongs to the controlled analytical method.
This is an interpretation principle, not a prescription for acidifying an
unknown extract: reactive metal residues and cyanide or sulfide species
require
trained laboratory supervision and suitable controls.
Precipitate colour or a single reagent observation is supporting evidence
rather than a unique identity.
Separate the conversion step, removal of interference and detection reaction
before assigning an element from the final observation.
One precipitate mass is not enough to determine two independent halide amounts
unless another measurement or constraint is supplied.
Consider a stipulated chloride and bromide mixture that forms only silver
chloride and silver bromide quantitatively.
An independent determination gives total halide amount three point zero zero
millimoles, while the dry mixed precipitate mass is zero point four seven five
zero gram.
Use the supplied rounded molar masses one hundred forty three point five for
silver chloride and one hundred eighty eight point zero grams per mole for
silver bromide.
If all three millimoles were chloride, the precipitate mass would be zero
point
four three zero five gram.
The actual excess mass is zero point zero four four five gram.
Replacing one mole silver chloride by one mole silver bromide raises mass by
forty four point five grams, so bromide amount is one point zero zero
millimole.
Chloride is the remaining two point zero zero millimoles.
The result assumes the named precipitates are pure and fully recovered, with
no
interfering silver compounds or retained liquid.
Preserve the independent total amount constraint; a heavier precipitate alone
does not uniquely reveal mixture composition.
Selective crystallization uses different solubilities, but high crystal purity
does not require complete recovery of the desired compound.
In a stipulated ideal model, a hot solution contains ten point zero grams
desired solid A and two point zero grams soluble impurity B in fifty point
zero
grams water.
On cooling, the supplied solubilities are four point zero grams A and eight
point zero grams B per one hundred grams water.
The liquid can retain two point zero grams A and up to four point zero grams
B.
Thus eight point zero grams A crystallize while all two grams B can remain
dissolved.
With no co crystallization or trapped liquid, the crystals are pure A in this
model, but recovery is only eighty percent of the original A.
A separate fresh ten gram cold water wash that reaches the stated solubility
can dissolve another zero point four gram A.
Remaining crystals are seven point six grams, or seventy six percent overall
recovery.
Real washing may not reach equilibrium, and crystal occlusion or mixed solids
can affect purity.
These are supplied mass balance assumptions, not guarantees of an experimental
separation or a solvent handling procedure.
Distillation separates a mixture because the vapour can have a different
composition from the liquid in equilibrium with it.
For a supplied ideal binary liquid, let the liquid mole fraction of A be zero
point two five zero and that of B zero point seven five zero.
At the stated common temperature, take pure component vapour pressures one
hundred kilopascals for A and forty kilopascals for B.
Raoult's law gives partial pressures twenty five and thirty kilopascals, with
total pressure fifty five.
In an ideal vapour mixture, A therefore has mole fraction twenty five divided
by fifty five, or about zero point four five five.
This exceeds its liquid fraction, so the vapour is enriched in the more
volatile component A.
It is not pure A, and its mole fraction is not the same as its mass fraction
without molar mass information.
Repeated equilibration can improve separation in an appropriate fractional
distillation model.
Actual mixtures may be nonideal or form azeotropes, so repeated stages do not
guarantee arbitrary purity for every liquid pair.
State temperature, ideality and both phase compositions before interpreting a
distillation question.
An extraction coefficient must distinguish one neutral species from all
analytical forms of an acid.
In a supplied supporting model, neutral H A partitions between immiscible
organic and aqueous phases with coefficient P equal to ten, defined as organic
neutral concentration divided by aqueous neutral concentration.
Its ionized form A minus stays in water.
At maintained aqueous p H and acid constant p K a four, the ratio of aqueous
ionized to neutral acid is ten raised to p H minus p K a.
The total analytical distribution ratio D is therefore P divided by one plus
that ratio.
At p H four, D is five.
With one hundred millilitres aqueous phase and fifty millilitres organic
phase,
the equilibrium fraction of the acid inventory in organic solution is five
times fifty divided by one hundred plus five times fifty, or five sevenths,
about seventy one point four percent.
At p H six, D drops to ten over one hundred one, and the fraction falls to
about four point seven two percent.
This assumes maintained p H, no organic ion transfer, no association and
unchanged phase volumes; it is a specified equilibrium model, not a universal
solvent preference or experimental procedure.
Chromatography requires naming both phases and the retention mechanism, rather
than treating every chromatogram as the same process.
In a stipulated normal phase thin layer model, polar silica is the stationary
solid and a relatively nonpolar liquid is the mobile phase.
A compound that interacts more strongly with the silica spends less time
moving
with the solvent and can show a lower retention factor.
Suppose under the same run conditions sample A travels one point two five
centimetres, sample B three point seven five, and the solvent front five point
zero zero.
Their retention factors are zero point two five and zero point seven five.
The observations are consistent with stronger retention of A in that system,
not a universal molecular polarity measurement.
A more strongly eluting mobile phase often competes more effectively for
adsorption sites and changes both movements.
In a simple partition chromatography teaching model, retention instead follows
distribution between a stationary liquid and the moving phase; water
associated
with paper can play that stationary liquid role.
Real surfaces can involve mixed interactions.
State the model, solvent and stationary material before predicting a direction
or transferring a ranking to another chromatographic system.
A wet sample and an instrumental blank contribute different masses to a
combustion analysis.
Consider a supplied sample of zero point five zero zero zero gram with
independently measured water content zero point zero five zero zero gram.
Dry analyte mass is therefore zero point four five zero zero gram.
Collected carbon dioxide is zero point six eight zero zero gram, including a
reagent blank of zero point zero two zero zero, so analyte carbon dioxide is
zero point six six zero zero gram.
Using carbon twelve and carbon dioxide forty four gives zero point one eight
zero zero gram carbon, or forty percent on the dry basis.
Collected water is zero point three two nine zero gram.
Subtract its zero point zero zero nine zero blank and the sample's original
zero point zero five zero zero water, leaving zero point two seven zero zero
gram water produced from analyte hydrogen.
That corresponds to zero point zero three zero zero gram hydrogen.
If the dry compound contains only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, oxygen by
difference is zero point two four zero zero gram, and the empirical ratio is
one to two to one.
The formula is C H two O; a molecular formula still needs molar mass evidence.
Sublimation can separate a suitably volatile solid from a much less volatile
impurity without requiring a stable liquid intermediate.
Solid molecules enter the vapour phase and can deposit again as solid
elsewhere.
In an appropriate comparison, camphor is much more volatile than sodium
chloride, so this property can support a separation.
The method still needs adequate vapour pressure and chemical stability; a
compound that decomposes is not automatically purified merely because material
appears at another location.
Mechanical entrainment or another volatile impurity can contaminate the
collected fraction.
In a supplied recovery ledger, an initial mixture contains two point zero zero
grams desired solid.
A collected fraction has total mass one point five zero grams and independent
assay gives ninety six point zero percent desired compound.
Recovered analyte is one point four four grams, giving seventy two point zero
percent recovery.
Dividing one point five zero directly by two point zero zero would give
seventy
five percent, but would count impurity as product.
Purity describes the composition of the collected fraction; recovery describes
the desired amount retained from the original inventory.
This is interpretation of phase behaviour and assay data, not an apparatus or
heating procedure.
